newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Corporate Australia to reap benefits of low rates.
newsitem.headline: Corporate Australia to reap benefits of low rates.

text.p: The Australian corporate bond market is set to reap benefits from the latest Reserve Bank's interest rate cut to 5.0 percent on Wednesday.
Market analysts said corporate borrowers had been waiting for the rate cut before taking advantage of attractive borrowing and arbitrage opportunities.

Rating agency Standard & Poor's Corp also believes the strong volumes of securitised debt experienced in the first half of 1997 will lead to increasing depth and liquidity, another attraction for investment in non-government debt.
John Crooks, Societe Generale's senior manager capital markets, fixed income, said corporations had expected the rate cut and were holding back from borrowing until it was delivered.
Crooks said corporate Australia's reaction to the rate cut and the prospect of further rate cuts should be seen in the next couple of days.
However, ANZ Investment Bank analyst Jason Carley believes the prospect of a further monetary policy easing would not deter investors in the corporate bond market.
"We will see corporate bonds becoming more and more attractive as absolute yields of all government debt goes down further," Carley said.
"The rate cut equals increased investment in the corporate bond market," Carley said. "It will encourage the market to look at corporate bonds for borrowings."

An official from JP Morgan maintains that the attraction for spread products is the basis of the predicted growth in the corporate bond market, as spreads for government financial instruments have narrowed significantly.
"The rate cut caused the government and bond market to rally and interest rates to decrease," he said. "Lowered interest rates mean investors will be hungry for spread products."
He also said the Australian swap market would experience an increase in activity.
"Corporates would be looking to fix interest rates in the swap market," he said. "This will in effect move swap spreads giving better arbitrage opportunities for issuers."
S&P expects the securitisation market will also experience the highest volume on record in second half 1997.

"In Australia, strong volumes of mortgage and asset-backed securities issued in the first six months of 1997 have created more efficient markets with increasing depth and liquidity in the trading of these securities, giving issuers greater incentive to tap local capital markets," S&P said in a report.
"We expect an ever increasing volume of new ratings for the second half of 1997, with new issues expected to hit a record high," the rating agency added.
Adding to the positive outlook for non-government debt was the upgrade of Australia's lowest rated issuer, Brierley Investments Ltd, to BBB from BBB-minus on Wednesday.
ANZ Investment Bank's Carley believes this is very positive to the Australian corporate bond market and would encourage people to look at corporate bonds for borrowings.
